props.title: Roberta
props.initialSlug: Musical comedy with mistaken identity in Paris

sections.content: Roberta marks a pivotal moment in Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers' partnership, coming right after their breakout in The Gay Divorcee (1934). This sophisticated musical romance set in Paris showcases their evolving chemistry, with Irene Dunne adding exceptional vocal talent. The film's fashion house setting allows for stunning Art Deco designs and glamorous costumes that defined RKO's distinctive 1930s style. While less famous than Top Hat (1935) or Swing Time (1936), Roberta delivers some of Astaire and Rogers' most elegant dance numbers, particularly their "I Won't Dance" routine.

sections.content: Jerome Kern's score for Roberta demonstrates how Hollywood musicals were evolving in the mid-1930s. The integration of "Smoke Gets in Your Eyes" - already a popular standard - shows the growing sophistication of the genre. Compare this to earlier musicals like 42nd Street (1933) or Gold Diggers of 1933 (1933), where songs were more directly staged as performance numbers. Roberta begins moving toward the more naturalistic style that would later define films like Meet Me in St. Louis (1944).

The film's handling of fashion and European sophistication established a template that later films would follow, from Funny Face (1957) to The Devil Wears Prada (2006). The Paris setting, haute couture backdrop, and emphasis on style and elegance created a distinct atmospheric approach that influenced countless Hollywood productions, particularly in how they portrayed the fashion industry and European cultural sophistication. sections.content: Roberta's costume design by Bernard Newman represents the height of 1930s Hollywood glamour. The film's fashion show sequence particularly influenced later productions like Cover Girl (1944) and Easter Parade (1948). The way the film integrates fashion with narrative anticipates later works like An American in Paris (1951), where style and setting become crucial storytelling elements rather than mere window dressing.
